sections.name: Full-bleed roofing hero, parallax image + staggered headline
sections.notes: Fixed-position hero image creates a parallax effect as the page scrolls under it (JS toggles .is-past once scrolled out of the viewport — not included here, degrades gracefully to a static bg). Headline lines and CTAs fade/slide in via .intro-in class added on load; .no-js fallback keeps everything visible with no JS. Image is a shared library placeholder (assets/placeholders/exterior-home.jpg) — swap in the target site's own photo before shipping.

sections.name: Draggable horizontal review carousel with reply cards
sections.notes: Reviews are fabricated for this library — de-identified from the original client build and rewritten as fake, generic testimonials (swap in the target business's own real reviews before reuse). The reply line under each card — owner responding by name — is the standout trust device here; worth reusing even without the carousel. Horizontal scroll uses a CSS mask to fade the edges instead of hard-clipping cards; JS drag-to-scroll (grab/grabbing cursor) not included but the CSS supports it as pure scroll-snap too.

sections.name: Featured-service spotlight + compact grid of secondary services
sections.notes: Two-tier services pattern: one large 'specialty' feature card (image + long copy + capability list + link to its own page) alongside a compact grid of the remaining services as smaller cards. Good reference whenever a business has one flagship service worth showcasing and several supporting ones that don't need equal real estate.

sections.name: Split hero with rotating slide gallery and botanical line-art accents
sections.notes: Copy sits left, a fading slideshow of portrait-orientation photos sits right — good pattern for photographers/creatives where the images ARE the pitch. Inline SVG botanical sprigs (referenced via <use href="#bot-...">) are decorative flourishes defined once in a sprite sheet elsewhere on the page; this fragment references them by id but doesn't include the sprite defs. Uses <picture>/srcset for responsive art direction.

sections.name: Segmented pricing packages by client type (tiers within categories)
sections.notes: Not a single price ladder — instead groups by WHO the client is (Families, Solos & Graduates, etc.) and shows 1-2 price tiers inside each group. Good reference for service businesses whose pricing varies more by customer segment than by feature tier. data-reveal attributes hook into an intersection-observer fade-in (script not included).

sections.name: Split hero with trust badge, overlapping stat card, and plank texture accent
sections.notes: Stat card (years in business / review count / rating) overlaps the hero image corner rather than living in its own section — keeps proof visible without adding vertical scroll. data-count-to attributes are hooks for a count-up-on-scroll script (not included, degrades to static numbers). No webfont dependency — deliberately system-font for a fast, plain-spoken feel matching the trade.

sections.name: Minimal centered dark CTA banner
sections.notes: About as simple as a closing CTA gets: headline, one line of support copy, a phone-call button and a secondary quote-request button. Useful as a mid-page or pre-footer breather section when a full contact form section would be too heavy. Smallest file in the library — good starting point to restyle rather than strip down.

sections.name: Full-bleed hero with animated line-by-line headline and live open/closed status
sections.notes: Three one-word headline lines ('Climbed.' 'Cut.' 'Cleared.') each animate in on their own line — punchy rhythm pattern worth reusing for trades with a clear step-by-step process. Has a commented-out slot for swapping the still image for a looping background video once the client supplies footage. data-status/data-status-text hooks are for a live business-hours widget (JS not included, static fallback text shown as-is).

sections.name: Combined proof section: animated stat row + award plaque + Google rating summary
sections.notes: Stacks three proof devices in one section instead of spreading them thin: a stat row (years/reviews/rating/awards, count-up-on-scroll hooks via data-count), a photographed award plaque with a bulleted achievement list, and a Google-rating summary block (real G logo SVG inlined) with an HTML comment marking where to drop in a live Elfsight/Trustindex/Featurable review-widget embed later. Heaviest file in the library — good candidate to split back into 2-3 smaller sections if only one device is needed.

sections.name: Luxury full-bleed hero with badge, glow overlay, and location pin
sections.notes: Layers a subtle radial 'glow' div over the standard image+gradient hero for extra shine — cheap way to make a dark hero feel premium/detailing-shop rather than flat. HTML comment marks exactly what the hero image should be before an asset existed yet, worth keeping as a habit when spec-building ahead of client photos.

sections.name: Simple centered CTA banner with label tag and phone/book buttons
sections.notes: Same job as 0007 (the plain-spoken trade CTA) but with a small uppercase label-tag above the headline and .fade-up scroll-reveal hooks — compare the two side by side for 'plain trade CTA' vs 'polished premium-service CTA' at nearly the same structure.

sections.name: Brutalist hero: framed grid, safety-yellow signal color, mono type
sections.notes: Original build for the library, not adapted from a client site — a deliberately unpolished, structural counterpoint to the softer heroes elsewhere here. Hairline 1.5px borders (--border-w) replace shadows/radius entirely (every element has border-radius:0 forced via a wildcard rule) — everything reads as poured, not styled. The stat row's rules run continuous across the full width on top and bottom only, with no vertical dividers between stats — keep it that way rather than boxing each stat individually. The single safety-yellow accent (--signal) is the only color allowed to break the black/paper/concrete palette; don't dilute it by adding a second accent. Image gets grayscale+contrast filter to read as raw print rather than a photo. -webkit-text-stroke outline on one headline word (.outline) is a Chrome/Safari/Firefox-only effect — falls back to solid fill elsewhere, still legible.

sections.name: Luxury hero: split marble portrait, gold hairlines, italic serif
sections.notes: Original build for the library, not adapted from a client site — restraint is the whole design: one accent (gold), one weight of hairline (1px), generous whitespace instead of visual noise. Ring-monogram + tracked wordmark reads as a badge/seal rather than a logo lockup — reuse that device for other high-end sections (real estate, private practice, bespoke goods, weddings) rather than the botanical/floral device already used for the softer 'elegant' family (0004/0005). Footnote row (Est./By Referral/Rating) is a credibility device that works instead of a stat row when the brand's positioning is scarcity/exclusivity rather than scale.

sections.name: Dynamic hero: diagonal gradient, skewed badges, clipped action photo
sections.notes: Original build for the library, not adapted from a client site — built for a startup/fitness/events-type brand that wants to feel fast rather than trustworthy-and-steady. Every skewed element (badges, buttons, media tag) uses the same -8deg transform with an inner un-skewed span so the text itself stays readable — copy that exact pattern rather than skewing text directly, which garbles it. The clip-path on .hero__media only applies above 900px; below that it's a plain full-width image, since an angled clip on a short mobile viewport just crops the photo awkwardly. Three-stop diagonal gradient (violet→magenta→orange) is the accent system here instead of a single accent color — keep all three stops if reusing, dropping to two reads flatter and less 'in motion.'

sections.name: Brutalist hero (mobile-fit): paper + terracotta, no-scroll on any device
sections.notes: Second brutalist hero — paired with 0012 as the same design language in a different register: light paper ground instead of black, terracotta signal instead of safety-yellow, condensed Bebas Neue instead of blocky Archivo Black, a different real photo (a graphic architectural roofline, not a concrete building). Built specifically so every element — header, image, headline, dek, CTAs, stat row — is visible on one mobile screen with zero scrolling: the whole layout is a single-column flex column pinned to height:100svh, and every font-size/padding/gap uses a clamp() with an svh component so it scales down on short viewports instead of overflowing. Tested down to 375×667 (iPhone SE-class, the shortest common phone viewport) with room to spare; taller/wider viewports just get more breathing room via justify-content:center, not more content. If you add copy, keep the headline to one short line plus one accent word, and the dek to 1-2 short sentences — this layout has no scroll fallback, so it depends on staying terse.

sections.name: Marketing agency hero: large centered headline permanently clipped to an inverted-color window of a city-lights photo, shifting as the page scrolls
sections.notes: Every line of the headline is masked now — no plain fallback line. Each h1 span sets background-image to the same hero photo, background-clip:text, then filter:invert(1) saturate(1.3) contrast(1.3) brightness(1.2), so the letters read as a bright inverted-color 'window' cut into the dark photo behind them, permanently on. Runs on city-lights-night.jpg (a starry night skyline with saturated red/teal/blue reflections) because the color variety and inverted starfield read as literal texture through the letters; pick a similarly high-contrast, colorful night/light-source photo if swapping it out, not a flat daylight shot. background-size is auto 230% (not plain 'cover') with background-position center 62% — at most hero aspect ratios 'cover' shows this photo's full height with no vertical crop room, which parks the top headline line over the empty near-black sky (inverts to near-flat white, reading as if the mask were 'off'); zooming in and biasing toward 62% keeps every line over the busy skyline/reflection band instead, so the invert effect stays visibly on everywhere the heading sits. Both image layers are pinned to the viewport rather than scrolling with the page — .hero-bg is position:fixed and .mask-heading span uses background-attachment:fixed — so as the page scrolls, the pinned crop stays put while the headline (normal in-flow content) slides over it, and each letter reveals a different part of the same image as it moves past. Verified via getComputedStyle(...).position/backgroundAttachment staying 'fixed' at multiple scroll positions, and the visible crop behind the letters visibly changing as hero-main scrolls up over the still-pinned background. .hero-main is align-items:center + text-align:center and the heading's clamp() runs up to 11rem — deliberately large and centered. The old dark linear-gradient shadow over the photo (.hero::after) is gone entirely so the city itself reads bright and clear; non-masked text (eyebrow, dek, ghost button, foot stats) got text-shadow and/or a small blurred dark pill background instead, scoped to just that text. Both fixed layers fall back to normal scroll under 720px width and prefers-reduced-motion. A second '.scroll-demo' section (paper background, 3-column capability grid) is appended after the hero purely so this file has something to scroll into on its own — it's explicitly commented as library-only and should be deleted when pulling the hero into a real page, which otherwise supplies its own next section. Confirmed the pinned .hero-bg doesn't bleed through onto that later section (a real risk with position:fixed inside an isolation:isolate ancestor in some render paths) by scrolling past the hero in a fresh preview tab and checking the paper section renders opaque on top, not underneath the pinned photo.

sections.name: Marketing agency hero: split layout with a giant slow-rotating conic pinwheel filling the right side
sections.notes: No photo in this one on purpose — the .pinwheel is a pure CSS conic-gradient (no image, no SVG, no JS) spun with a 34s linear infinite rotation, plus a dashed ring inside it counter-rotating at 22s for depth. Both are pure decoration built from CSS custom properties, so recoloring the target site's brand is a two-variable swap (--violet, --lime). If pulling into a real build with a photo-driven identity, either drop the photo into .hero-motion behind the pinwheel at reduced opacity, or keep it photo-free — it reads fine either way. Respects prefers-reduced-motion by killing both rotations outright rather than slowing them, since a giant frozen pinwheel still reads fine as a static graphic.

sections.name: Marketing agency hero: dark full-bleed with blurred gradient blobs that drift toward the cursor
sections.notes: No photo — three blurred radial-gradient circles (mix-blend-mode:screen) are the whole background. Inline script listens for pointermove on the section, lerps each blob's translate3d toward the cursor at its own 'data-depth' speed (0.06 easing factor per frame via requestAnimationFrame) so the blobs trail with a soft parallax lag rather than snapping to the pointer; on pointerleave they drift back to center. Each blob also runs its own independent CSS scale-pulse keyframe so it's never fully static even with the mouse away, but the JS transform and the CSS pulse are on separate nested elements (.blob for JS translate, .blob-core for the CSS animation) specifically so they don't stomp the same transform property. Script self-skips entirely under prefers-reduced-motion (checked once on load) and the CSS also kills the pulse keyframes for that case — touch devices simply get the idle pulse with blobs centered, which still looks intentional. A light grain overlay (radial-gradient dot pattern) keeps the blur from looking like a cheap Photoshop glow.

sections.name: Marketing agency hero: two tilted, counter-scrolling outline-text marquee belts of service names over a marble photo
sections.notes: Two .marquee-row belts, each slightly counter-rotated (-2.2deg / +2deg) so they read as crossing banners rather than a flat ticker. Each belt's .marquee-track content is duplicated exactly twice back-to-back, then animated translateX(0) to translateX(-50%) linear infinite — that exact duplication is what makes the loop seamless; changing the word list means keeping both copies identical or the seam will jump. Rows scroll opposite directions (second uses animation-direction:reverse plus a different duration) so they don't read as a single mechanical strip. Every other word is outline-only (-webkit-text-stroke, transparent fill) and every other word solid gold (.solid) — that alternation is what keeps a wall of giant type legible instead of a solid block. Belt sits between the eyebrow and the dek/CTA, not behind the headline, so it never fights with body copy for contrast. animation set to none (not paused) under prefers-reduced-motion, per the marquee text still being readable as a static line either way.

sections.name: Marketing agency hero: split editorial hero, headline's last word cycles through four outcomes on a pure-CSS relay
sections.notes: Pure CSS relay, no JS. Four .cycle-word spans are absolutely stacked inside a fixed-height .cycle wrapper; each runs the same 9.6s cycleWord keyframe but with animation-delay staggered by 2.4s (9.6s / 4 words), so only one word is ever visible at a time in a continuous hand-off loop. To add/remove a word: change both the delay stagger (cycle-duration / word-count) on the nth-child selectors AND the keyframe's percentages stay the same since they're relative to each word's own delayed timeline, not the total word count — only the delay math needs to change. Reduced-motion fallback hides every word but the first and kills the animation, so it reads as a normal static headline rather than four overlapping words. Swap portrait-lifestyle.jpg for the target site's actual founder/team photo — the rounded 'Since 2016' badge pairs best with a personal, founder-led positioning; drop it if the target brand doesn't lead with a specific date.

sections.name: Marketing agency hero: dot-grid background with a cursor-tracked radial spotlight that lights up a brighter acid-green grid underneath
sections.notes: Two identical dot-grid layers stacked: .grid-dim is always-visible at low opacity, .grid-bright is the same grid in acid-green clipped by a CSS mask-image radial-gradient centered on --spot-x/--spot-y — those two custom properties are updated on every pointermove via inline script (hero.style.setProperty), so the bright grid only shows in a ~260px circle around the cursor, like a flashlight over a PCB. No canvas, no per-frame JS loop — the mask just tracks the custom properties directly, so it's as cheap as a CSS transition. Under prefers-reduced-motion the script sets a fixed spot position once and never attaches the pointermove listener, so the bright patch just sits static near the headline instead of chasing a cursor that convention says shouldn't be implied. The floating .proof-card (client headshot + stat) is what stops this hero from reading as pure dev-tool aesthetic — don't drop it without replacing it with some other human/credibility element, or the section reads cold for a marketing (not SaaS) audience.

sections.name: Marketing agency hero: split layout with three vertical columns of work thumbnails auto-scrolling at different speeds and directions
sections.notes: Three .reel-col columns, each an overflow:hidden window over a .reel-track whose image list is duplicated exactly twice, translateY(0) to translateY(-50%) linear infinite — identical loop mechanism to the horizontal marquee in 0019, just on the Y axis. Middle column runs animation-name:scrollDown (translateY(-50%) to 0, i.e. visually descending) so the three columns don't move in lockstep; third column reuses scrollUp but at a slower 44s duration for a third distinct speed. A mask-image linear-gradient fades the top and bottom ~10% of the .reel container so no image is ever seen 'popping' at a hard edge. This is a placeholder reel — the six placeholder images per column are just the library's five stock photos cycled for visual variety; a real build swaps every image for that agency's actual case-study thumbnails (keep each track's list duplicated exactly once for the loop math to stay seamless when the count changes). Reduced motion freezes all three tracks in their default stacked position rather than trying to show a 'representative' single frame.

sections.name: Marketing agency hero: headline scrambles through random characters on load before decoding into the final words
sections.notes: Each [data-scramble] node runs its own requestAnimationFrame loop: over 900ms it locks characters left-to-right (Math.floor(progress*len) determines how many characters from the start are 'solved') while every unsolved character is re-randomized from CHARS on every single frame, giving the classic terminal-decode look. The two headline lines are staggered 450ms apart (scramble(node, 150 + i*450)) so the second line starts decoding just as the first is finishing, not simultaneously. Script sets each node's textContent to a fully-scrambled string synchronously before scheduling the animation, so there's no flash-of-final-text before JS runs. Under prefers-reduced-motion the whole IIFE returns early and the original textContent (already the final copy, since data-scramble mirrors it) is left untouched — no scrambling happens at all rather than a slowed-down version. The pulsing cyan 'Decoding audience signal' status dot in the top bar is a second, independent nod to the same motif and can be swapped for a real live-status indicator (open/closed, live chat, etc.) per the pattern in section 0008.

sections.name: Marketing agency hero: canvas particle field that resolves into the headline, morphs between words, and parts around the cursor
sections.notes: The most technically involved section in the library — read this before touching it. The headline is not text: each word is rasterised to an offscreen canvas, read back with getImageData, and every pixel with alpha>128 on a 4px grid becomes a particle target. A single particle pool sized to the LONGEST word is reused across all words; particles a shorter word doesn't need go inactive and drift at 22% alpha as background dust (that dust is the effect, not a bug — it's what makes 'RESULTS' look like the residue of 'ATTENTION'). Targets are shuffled before assignment so letters fill in organically rather than scanline-by-scanline. Physics is a plain spring (vx += (goal-x)*0.055, damped *0.86) plus a cursor repulsion field that punches a visible hole through the word and lets it heal; pointerdown scatters the whole field and the springs reassemble it. CRITICAL: sampling runs only after document.fonts.load('400 100px "Anton"') resolves — sampling before the webfont lands rasterises a fallback face and the entire headline comes out the wrong shape, which is the single easiest way to break this section. Font size is derived by measuring the word at 100px and scaling to 86% of canvas width, so it fits any container without hardcoded breakpoints. SAMPLE_GAP is the density/performance dial (4 ≈ 4-5.7k particles here; raise it to 6 on a page that already runs other animation). Canvas is aria-hidden with a real .sr-only <h1> carrying the copy, since canvas text is invisible to screen readers and search engines — keep that pairing if you reuse this. Under prefers-reduced-motion the rAF loop never starts and drawStatic() paints one settled word.

sections.name: Marketing agency hero: photo physically warped by animated SVG turbulence, copy sitting on a morphing gooey metaball panel
sections.notes: Two SVG filters carry this section, both defined in an inline <svg class="svg-defs"> that must stay in the DOM for the filter: url(#id) references to resolve. (1) #liquidWarp: feTurbulence feeds feDisplacementMap over the photo, so the image is genuinely warped, not overlaid. The perf trick that makes it viable: JS writes feDisplacementMap@scale every frame (cheap — the noise raster is cached) but only nudges feTurbulence@baseFrequency on every 4th frame (expensive — it forces the noise to re-render). Measured 60fps at 1440x900 with that split; remove the throttle and it drops hard. Pointer SPEED (not position) feeds an 'energy' value that spikes the displacement scale up to ~67 and decays at 0.955/frame, so a flick churns the surface and it settles back to a slow resting ripple. (2) #gooMerge: blur + an alpha-crushing feColorMatrix fuses the three .goo-blob circles into one organic mass that morphs as they orbit on offset CSS durations (17s/13s/21s, all 'alternate', so the merge pattern never visibly repeats). The blobs MUST be opaque (#0b0a08) — the goo matrix destroys soft alpha, so transparency comes from .goo-layer's opacity instead. That mass is also the legibility device: the photo sits at brightness 1.05 rather than being dimmed globally, and the goo is what buys contrast under the copy, which is why the blobs are sized in vw (not vmin — with vmin they shrink away from the text as the window widens and the copy falls off the dark area). The photo overhangs its frame by 9% on every side because the displacement drags pixels inward and would otherwise pull transparent gaps in at the edges. Under prefers-reduced-motion the rAF loop never starts, scale is pinned to a static 10, and every CSS animation including the liquid-metal text sheen is disabled.

sections.name: Marketing agency hero: real CSS 3D scene with depth-layered parallax and a rotating cylinder of service words orbiting the copy
sections.notes: Genuine 3D, not simulated parallax: .stage sets perspective:1100px, .scene is preserve-3d and rotates on two axes, and four .layer elements sit at real translateZ depths (-520 photo, -300 grid, -250 ring, +95 chips). The parallax is a free consequence of perspective — there are no per-layer movement multipliers anywhere, which is the point. Each layer counter-scales by P/(P−z) so it reads at its intended size despite its depth; if you change a translateZ you MUST change the matching scale or that layer will visibly jump size. JS writes four custom properties (--rx/--ry/--px/--py) and CSS consumes them; it also shifts perspective-origin, not just rotation, which is what makes it feel like looking around a scene rather than tipping a flat card. Tilt is eased at 0.08/frame toward the target and the rAF loop self-terminates once it settles (no idle loop burning frames). MAX_TILT is 7deg — past about 9 the perspective distortion gets seasick. The word cylinder is 10 <b> elements at 36deg intervals, each rotateY(n) translateZ(15em); radius is in em so it tracks the font size. Two things to know if you re-tune it: backface-visibility:hidden is what stops the far half of the cylinder rendering mirrored/reversed, and the ring deliberately lives in its own band at top:72% rather than centred — centred it hides behind the headline and reads as stray fragments at the edges, so .hero-core carries extra bottom padding to open that band up. Measured 60fps at 1440x900. Under prefers-reduced-motion the script returns before binding anything, the scene transform is cleared, and the ring parks at a static -18deg so it still reads as a dimensional object.
